body.heading: Go early
paragraphs: On a cool morning, go outside with your adult before the sun gets warm. Look in bushes, fences, and corners for spider webs covered in tiny drops.
The drops are dew. Water in the cool night air lands on the web and turns it into a string of tiny jewels.

body.heading: Look at the pattern
paragraphs: Every web is built to a pattern. Lines run out from the middle like the spokes of a bicycle wheel, and more lines spiral around them.
The spider built all of this in the dark, using its own silk. The silk comes from inside the spider's body and is stronger than you would guess.

body.heading: Leave it shining
paragraphs: By lunchtime, the sun will dry the drops away and the web will be hard to see again. The spider does not mind — it only needs the web, not the jewels.
Say thank you to the spider for the morning show and leave its home exactly as you found it.

takeaway: Morning dew turns spider webs into jewel strings, and looking without touching keeps the spider's home safe.
materials: A magnifying glass if you have one
safetyNotes: Look at webs without touching them — a web is a spider's home and its way of catching food. Never touch a spider.
screenFreeExtension: Draw your own web with a white crayon, then paint over it with watery paint to make it appear.
